I have previously written about my concerns about “politicized psychiatry” in support of cannabis prohibition and the broader “therapeutic state”.

See

Politicized Psychiatry Is Insane

And

How Politicized Psychiatry and Bad Journalism Combined to Make It Easy for Me. Two Articles for the Price of One

And

Politicized Psychiatry and the Rehab Rackets

 

Until recently, I had not written about one of the foremost practitioners of this “art”, Mark S. Gold, M.D., “a pioneering researcher, professor, and chairman of psychiatry at Yale, the University of Florida, and Washington University in St Louis.”

 

But then he decided to add to the recent Prohibitionist extravaganza around a really absurd series of articles about THC in drivers killed in automobile accidents, published in  Psychology Today..

 

His was one of the more professional examples. (Faint praise)

So I responded with Critique of “Weed, THC, Car Crashes, and Fatalities”

 

I was amazed to find that apparently no one had ever observed that while cannabis use has gone up since 1992, automobile crash fatalities have gone down every year since then, except during the pandemic. If cannabis use is such a menace to the country, where are the bodies?

 

In any case, I decided to check back with Psychology Today to see if I was missing anything, and there was The Many Risks of Cannabis and High-Dose THC Use Brain and behavioral effects on teens and young adults are of special concern.

 

Boring! I have been writing about that for decades.

See

The Perils of Potent Pot Party Line: Blaming Marijuana Legalization for Increase in THC Levels

And from 2007

The Iron Law of Prohibition: Potent Pot, New Data and the Old Prohibitionist Party Line and Another Lie.

 

But I just had to look, and there it was, my own gold standard for intellectual dishonesty, “The FDA has not approved the cannabis plant for any medical use.”

 

Of course, that is literally true, but in the middle of a “debate” about whether the DEA should even allow the debate over the rescheduling of “marijuana” he ignored this fact and instead treats it as evidence that there are clinical reasons against its medical use. Obviously, most clinically useful drugs are actually dangerous, especially to children.

 

But then… there it was…

“Modern cannabis products contain higher concentrations of THC compared to traditional flowers (bud). Marijuana tested at Woodstock in 1969 was usually Cannabis sativa at 1% THC(tetrahydrocannabinol). Today's cannabis flower typically contains >15%”

 

There is one major problem with that statement… NO MARIJUANA WAS TESTED AT WOODSTOCK in1969!

 

First, TETRA HYDRO CANNABINOL wasn’t discovered until 1964 in Israel.

Second, it was not tested outside of a laboratory in the United States until 1972 after the passage of the Control Act in 1970.

Third, I defy anyone, including Dr. Gold, to find any such testing data.

 

Finally, I highly recommend that you see the film Woodstock, but try to imagine any meaningful testing of samples being done there on anything, even if there had been any way of doing it.

 

And it has been 56 years since Woodstock, so, so what? My car got 10 miles to the gallon.

 

I have smoked with some regularity since 1967 (2 years before Woodstock) and I at least know the data.

 

The economics of contraband, marijuana prohibition, encouraged stronger and stronger weed, and that is now a part of the culture that prohibition created.

 

I wrote this on September 11, 1998

Excerpt from

Marijuana Prohibition And Potency, Price And Safety Is Marijuana Stronger Now Than It Was Back In the 60s, When Everyone Thought It Was Harmless?

 

Lesson One: Data, data, who’s got the data?

Any time that someone compares today’s marijuana with that of the 1960’s – or Woodstock, which is a common reference point – you can know with absolute certainty that they are lying. There is simply no data – no data – on marijuana potency from the 1960s, much less from any one concert. The first testing of marijuana for THC did not begin until the early 1970s.’

 

Here it gets a little bit more complicated.

 

“In 1972, the first year of official government testing for the THC level, a small sample of marijuana of unknown origin, but probably Mexican, averaged only 0.18% THC. This is below the level of industrial hemp, but this number is often used as the base for comparison to justify the high multiples.

If a visitor to the US walked out of his hotel and met a homeless person dressed in rags, and insisted that this was the typical American, ignoring everyone else in sight, you would question the visitor’s judgement -- or integrity. In effect, that is what prohibitionists are doing when they use this 1972 government number. It requires persistent dishonesty.

In their book Marijuana Myths; Marijuana Facts, Zimmer and Morgan devote a short chapter to the data on marijuana potency. I recommend this book for many reasons, but this chapter alone is worth the price of the book.

In it they point out that in 1973 a private company PharmChem tested four times as many samples as the government, and the average potency was 1.62%. Did marijuana increase in potency tenfold in one year?

Also consider that one sample tested by PharmChem in 1975 was actually 14% THC, which was 20 times the average for the samples tested by the government that year.

Subsequently, private testing was prohibited, and for 20 years the only data has come from the government, but in 1980 the average potency from government testing was around 2% and has generally varied between 2 and 3% ever since.

In short, there is no data from the 60’s, and data from the 70’s does not support the notion that there was only low THC marijuana available.

THC levels have risen sharply, but the greatest increases have been concurrent with increased use.

 

Finally, let’s review the facts

1. There has never been a “standard” measure for cannabis THC potency. Some was swag and some was primo. We rolled pinners or fatties. We smoked more or we smoked less. We had seeds because we hadn’t heard about sinsemilla.  It has been fifty years since PharmChem tested the 14% primo. And…

2. Even today, the black market has more than half of the market, so the biggest problem is not that weed is too strong, but that the consumers cannot know what they are buying.

3. Legal alcohol stores sell 5% alcohol wine coolers and 95% EverClear.

4. It is easier to keep minors out of legal stores than away from contraband.
